packs.title: Collections, gardens and open paths
packs.promise: Look closely at city collections, compare garden forms and make original records of parks and historic architecture.

q.s: Build a small timeline from labeled vehicles.
st: Enter the open museum with admission and choose three displayed vehicles from different stated years. Stay in public gallery routes and leave vehicles untouched.
Record the displayed make, model if given, and year for each. Add one visible design detail such as wheel placement, body shape or seating arrangement.
Put your three records in chronological order. Identify one design feature that differs between an earlier and later vehicle; use the display to check any claimed technical function.
Give the timeline a short original caption explaining what your three examples show and one limit of such a small sample.

q.s: Make a sequence from a real shoreline view.
st: Choose an open shoreline-loop viewpoint where you can pause without blocking walkers. Record three actual features in different parts of the view, such as a path edge, water pattern and background form.
Make four original sketch panels or written scene descriptions: the approach, the close detail, the wider view and the departure. Use those actual features to link the panels.
Give each panel a brief caption in your own words. Keep imagined events separate from what you observed; no bird, reflection or weather condition is required.
Review the sequence from the same permitted path and revise one panel so its relationship to the shoreline is clearer.

q.s: Compare vegetation, a built detail and the river boundary.
st: Choose an open public path in the actual park and record three visible forms: vegetation, a path-side structure such as a bench or rail, and the river’s land boundary. Keep away from the water edge.
Describe each form through shape, material or texture visible from the path. A bare branch works; no flowers, species identification or readable plant label is required.
Make a three-row comparison of how those forms define the park’s space. Mark any idea about their function as your interpretation unless a posted source states it.
Choose one relationship between two forms and describe it in two sentences grounded in the actual view. Leave plants and structures as you found them.

packs.title: Two downtown afternoons
packs.promise: Connect downtown landmarks, public art, riverfront paths and an indoor garden through two walking afternoons.

q.s: Collect three relationships in one public artwork.
st: Find an open public path with a clear view of Space Whale and its calf. Keep enough distance to see the whole form without blocking people using the plaza.
Record one relationship between the two figures, one glass-panel color or light detail, and one visible connection in the steel structure. Describe what is actually visible in the current light.
Read the City collection record for the artists and materials. Add the artist names to your notes, keeping them separate from any meaning you assign to the work.
Arrange your three observations into a brief looking guide for a friend: overall form, material and connection. No bright sunlight, nighttime illumination or exact color is required.

q.s: Write an original response to a visible form.
st: From an open path, choose one sculpture in the garden and record three visible details: an outline, a material surface and the space around it. Copy its title or artist name only if an available label states them.
Assign a plain action word to each detail, such as bend, repeat or open. These are your responses, not a claim about the artist’s intention.
Write four original lines using the action words and a concrete observed detail in each line. Keep the writing on your own page; a performance or mark on the artwork is not required.
Look again and revise one line that could describe any sculpture. Note the specific detail that made the revision possible.

q.s: Map the library’s indoor garden through an original diagram.
st: Enter the open library and identify three publicly accessible reading-area viewpoints with different relationships to the indoor plants or open space. Do not enter staff areas or occupied booked rooms.

At each viewpoint, record one actual spatial detail and one reason it might suit a kind of reading, such as a short browse or longer concentration. These are your impressions, not claims about other readers.
Make a small original three-place diagram or written layout description using only what you could observe. Label it as your reading-area study, not an accurate floor plan or accessible route.
Choose one available permitted place and spend a minute looking at a book or your own notes. Add one revision to your diagram based on that closer observation.
